Sleep medicine · published research

Restless legs syndrome

Near-infrared light at leg or foot points reduced restless-legs symptom scores in small randomized studies. In a hemodialysis trial, the group difference was present immediately after treatment but was not maintained after treatment stopped.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Near-infrared light at leg or foot points reduced restless-legs symptom scores in small randomized studies. In a hemodialysis trial, the group difference was present immediately after treatment but was not maintained after treatment stopped.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Sleep medicine > Restless legs syndrome category contains three human randomized reports and no review, animal, or cell study. One trial enrolled hemodialysis patients, and two 2011 papers came from the same research group. Whether the two 2011 reports share participants is unclear.

Human and clinical evidence

A single-blind randomized trial allocated 60 hemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome to near-infrared light at leg and foot acupoints or control. Symptom severity improved immediately after treatment, but the between-group difference was not maintained after treatment ended (Mohammadi et al. 2018). Mitchell et al.'s randomized study of 34 people reported lower symptom scores after four weeks of near-infrared treatment, with some improvement still present at four-week follow-up (2011). A second paper compared two infrared devices in 25 participants; both groups improved, but it lacked a sham or untreated comparison (Mitchell et al. 2011). The two 2011 reports should not automatically be counted as independent cohorts.

Animal evidence

No animal study is listed for restless legs syndrome.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory study is listed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trials used near-infrared devices on leg or foot acupoints, with schedules lasting several weeks. Wavelength is the light's color band and influences tissue penetration. Different devices and the dialysis-specific sample limit generalization to other restless-legs populations.

Interpretation

Short-term symptom-score reductions are reported, but durability and the size of the sham-controlled effect remain uncertain. Independent trials should clarify whether benefits persist and whether they apply to people outside hemodialysis settings.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term symptom-score improvement with near-infrared light in small randomized trials Very low for lasting benefit after treatment stops or for broader restless-legs populations
Publications and records3 unique titles (exact Sleep medicine > Restless legs syndrome)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Three small human trials report lower symptom scores, including one sham-controlled hemodialysis study. Two 2011 papers from the same research group may include overlapping participants. Larger independent trials should use sham treatment, follow symptoms after treatment stops, and recruit people beyond specialized dialysis samples.
